patient_information: A 38-year-old European expatriate male, married for several years, living in Malawi. He looks healthy with no specific comorbidities mentioned.
chief_complaint: Progressive constipation and difficulty passing urine for the past 3 weeks.
history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced increasing abdominal pressure to pass urine, eventually passing only small amounts, associated with increasing lower abdominal discomfort, abnormal sensations in the groins and around the genitals, and some erectile dysfunction. He denied weakness, dysaesthesia, or loss of sensation in his legs, but noted abnormal walking, though he could not fully explain the abnormality. He had no backache. Over the past 2 months, he had unintentional weight loss of 8 kg and fatigue without fever or night sweats, which he attributed to stressful circumstances at work. One week prior to presentation, he noticed reddish discoloration of his urine without painful micturition or fever. He had previously completed a course of four different medications prescribed at a local clinic. There is no history of trauma, and his past medical history is unremarkable.
exposure_and_epidemiology: A 38-year-old European expatriate living in Malawi, who had swum regularly in Lake Malawi.
physical_exam: General examination showed no abnormalities except for a palpable bladder. Rectal examination revealed a low anal sphincter tone. Genital examination was normal. Neurological examination showed lively, symmetrical tendon reflexes in the legs without clonus or pathological plantar reflexes, and no other abnormalities.
labs_and_diagnostics: Urine microscopy at a local clinic identified Schistosoma haematobium eggs. An abdominal ultrasound scan after attempted micturition showed a large bladder residue without other abnormalities. Full blood count showed a normal absolute WBC of 9 × 10^9/L, a relative eosinophilia of 21.8% (reference range: 1-6%), and an absolute eosinophil count of 1.15 × 10^9/L (reference: <0.45 × 10^9/L). ALT was slightly elevated. Creatinine and CRP were normal. An HIV test and VDRL were negative. Microscopy of stool and urine samples were normal (after initial treatment). Serological tests for schistosomiasis were not available. An MRI scan of the spinal cord revealed an enhancing 1 cm large lesion at the anterior aspect of the conus, with associated high T2 signal representing oedema extending from the lower end of the conus to the level of T9. Additionally, nodular thickening of the urine bladder wall was observed at the base and posterior aspect.
differential_diagnosis: Initial differential diagnoses for a conus medullaris syndrome in a young man living in tropical Africa included spinal cord schistosomiasis (most important), spinal tuberculosis, a spinal abscess, neurosyphilis, a tumour, or metastases impinging on the conus medullaris. Other conditions like tuberculosis and metastatic cancer (e.g., from bladder carcinoma) were also considered for the spinal cord abnormalities.
management_and_clinical_course: Prior to presentation, he was treated with praziquantel, ciprofloxacin, buscopan, and bisacodyl for reddish urine. Subsequently, urinary catheterization was required for 2 weeks. He received a second course of praziquantel and a course of high-dose prednisolone, tapered off over 2 months. He made a full recovery and was well after more than 2 years of follow-up.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was an infection with Schistosoma haematobium, complicated by spinal cord schistosomiasis presenting as a conus syndrome. This was evidenced by the identification of Schistosoma haematobium eggs in urine, significant eosinophilia, and characteristic abnormalities on MRI scanning including an enhancing lesion at the conus medullaris and bladder wall thickening, along with a full recovery after treatment with praziquantel and high-dose prednisolone.
